items.title: UK GDPR, Article 5: Principles relating to processing of personal data
items.quote: The controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, paragraph 1
items.why: The binding rule. Two duties in one sentence: to comply, and to be able to show it. Wording of 5(2) is unchanged by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, which amended 5(1)(b) and (e) and added 5(3). Article 24(1), read in the same pass, repeats the duty to be able to demonstrate. No outstanding changes shown on the day checked.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 142: Information notices
items.quote: to be provided before the end of the period of 24 hours beginning when the notice is given
items.why: Source of the 24-hour figure (s.142(7): urgent notices). The words 'or documents' were inserted throughout on 19 August 2025 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.97, so the notice now reaches documents as well as information. 'Commission' substituted 30 September 2026. One unrelated Northern Ireland effect is shown as outstanding.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 146: Assessment notices
items.quote: make arrangements for an approved person to prepare a report on a specified matter
items.why: What a compulsory audit can demand: entry, documents, equipment, explanations, staff interviews and, since 5 February 2026 (2025 Act s.98; S.I. 2026/82), a report by an approved person paid for by the organisation (11A). Source of the seven-day figure (s.146(8)); under (9) the period can be shorter where a failure or offence is suspected.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 148A: Interview notices
items.quote: answer questions with respect to any matter relevant to the investigation
items.why: New power, in force 5 February 2026 (2025 Act s.100; S.I. 2026/82 reg. 2(s)). Applies only where a failure or offence is suspected. Reaches the controller, anyone who is or was employed by it, and anyone who is or was concerned in its management. Urgent notices: 24 hours.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 155: Penalty notices
items.quote: has failed to comply with an information notice, an assessment notice
items.why: Failure to comply with an information, assessment, interview or enforcement notice is itself a ground for a penalty; section 157(4), read in the same pass, sets the higher maximum for it. Degree of responsibility and of co-operation are listed factors. 'Interview notice' and paragraph (c) were inserted on 5 February 2026.

items.title: Data Protection Fining Guidance: Relevant aggravating or mitigating factors
items.locator: Sections 'The degree of responsibility of the controller or processor' and 'The degree of cooperation with the Commissioner'; footnotes 69-71
items.quote: The Commissioner considers that the ordinary duty of cooperation is required by law and meeting this standard is therefore not a mitigating factor.
items.why: How record-keeping and cooperation move a fine. Degree of responsibility is 'an aggravating factor or, at best, a neutral factor' unless the organisation went beyond its duties; delay and non-engagement may aggravate, or be treated as failure to comply with a notice (fn 71). Statutory guidance under DPA 2018 s.160. The page shows no date and no 'under review' banner; it still says 'the Commissioner' and does not mention interview notices.

items.title: Guide to accountability and governance
items.locator: Sections 'Why is accountability important?', 'What do we need to do?' and 'What documentation should we maintain?'; checklist
items.quote: if you can’t show good data protection practices, it may leave you open to fines and reputational damage
items.why: Source of the quotation. Sets out what evidence to keep: policies, contracts, records of processing, breach log, impact assessments, records of consent. Carries the 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; latest update shown is 5 February 2026. The old accountability framework address now redirects to the audit framework.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Artificial intelligence toolkit: Governance and accountability in AI
items.locator: Control measures on the privacy management framework, the DPIA, the audit programme and change management
items.quote: Evidence that senior management have seen and signed off the risks associated with using AI.
items.why: What the regulator's auditors look for in an AI system's file: senior sign-off, a completed impact assessment, audit reports, a log of changes and versions that is easy to locate. Carries the 'under review' banner; no publication date on the page, so the year is the year it was read. Data protection only.

items.title: A guide to ICO audits (version 1.5)
items.locator: pp. 3-4 (executive summary, compulsory audits), p. 7 ('Document review'), p. 8
items.quote: Prior to the audit we will request necessary policies and procedures that relate to the agreed scope areas from the organisation being audited.
items.why: What is asked for first: policy documents, staff guidance, training modules, risk registers, information asset registers, governance structures and records of processing; then interviews and testing of practice. Says most audits are consensual (s.129) and that compulsory ones use s.146. Does not mention the report power added in February 2026.

items.title: Information Commissioner's Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025/26 (HC 274)
items.locator: p. 65 ('Regulatory Assurance audits'); table p. 67; pp. 34, 59, 62-63
items.quote: we completed a total of 85 audits, risk reviews and follow-up work
items.why: Source of the figure: 85 in 2025/26 (54 audits, 31 follow-ups, p. 67) against 77 the year before. Also records eight UK GDPR penalty notices totalling £32,402,373 (p. 59) and that no data yet exist on use of the February 2026 powers (pp. 62-63). A correction slip of September 2026 amends reprimand figures only.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 30: Records of processing activities
items.quote: shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility
items.why: The specific record-keeping duty behind the general one in Article 5(2), and the first thing the regulator's auditors ask for. Each controller must record purposes, categories of people and data, recipients, transfers, erasure time limits and security measures; processors keep a parallel record; both must hand it over on request (para 4, now reading 'the Commission' from 30 September 2026). Para 5 exempts organisations with fewer than 250 staff unless the processing is risky, not occasional, or includes special category or criminal offence data, which most AI use will be. No outstanding effects shown. Cited elsewhere in the library for a different passage.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 148: Destroying or falsifying information and documents etc
items.quote: to destroy or otherwise dispose of, conceal, block or (where relevant) falsify all or part of the information, document, equipment or material
items.why: The criminal edge of the accountability file. Once an information notice or assessment notice has been given, it is an offence to destroy, hide, block or falsify what it covers, or to let that happen, intending to keep it from the regulator. The only defence is that the destruction would have happened anyway, which is far easier to show with a retention schedule that is followed. The first pass read this and left it out for space. Text reads 'Commission' from 30 September 2026; one unrelated Northern Ireland effect is shown as outstanding.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 12: Record-keeping
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 12(1)-(3); read with Art. 18 (documentation kept for 10 years) and Art. 19 (logs kept at least six months)
items.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
items.why: Record-keeping as a design requirement, which UK law does not impose in terms: a high-risk system must be built to log events automatically so that risks, monitoring and operation can be traced. Articles 18 and 19, read in the same pass, set how long documentation and logs are kept. It matches the criterion's fourth level, where the file is kept current by the system and not by hand. Unmarked on the page, so unchanged by the Digital Omnibus. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (EUR-Lex consolidation as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal; EUR-Lex itself returned an empty page. EU law: it reaches UK firms only where they place systems on the EU market or their output is used there. No application date is stated here because none was read on this page.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
items.locator: 'At a glance'; section 'What do we need to consider when undertaking data protection impact assessments for AI?'
items.quote: you still need to document how you have made this assessment
items.why: The regulator's AI-specific statement of what must be written down: how the organisation justified using AI at all, the impact assessment, the views of people consulted, trade-offs (for example accuracy against minimisation) with method and reasons, and, where it decides no impact assessment is needed, how it reached that view. Carries the banner: under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act. Date is the 'latest updates' date shown. Cited elsewhere in the library for other passages.

items.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
items.quote: the DPIA failed properly to assess the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects
items.why: A court testing an accountability file and finding it wanting. South Wales Police had written an impact assessment for live facial recognition; the Court of Appeal held it did not meet the statutory requirements because it wrongly assumed there was no interference with privacy rights, so it neither assessed the risks properly nor addressed measures to deal with them. The lesson is that a document existing is not enough; its reasoning is examined. Limits: law enforcement processing under Part 3 of the 2018 Act (section 64), not the UK GDPR Article 35 duty that applies to most firms, though the two are closely parallel.

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: guidance for public sector bodies
items.locator: Section 2 'ATRS purpose and scope'; sections 5-13 (the template fields); section 14
items.quote: It consists of a template for organisations to fill in with key information about their algorithmic tools.
items.why: The UK's only official template for a per-system record: owner, purpose, how the tool fits the decision process, human oversight, appeals, data, risks and impact assessments, kept up to date and published. Mandatory for government departments and certain arm's-length bodies; any organisation can use the fields as a contents list for its own file. Limits: public sector, a transparency record written for publication and not a full compliance file. Date is the 'updated' date shown. Cited elsewhere in the library for other passages.

items.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
items.publisher: Info-communications Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore
items.locator: p. 44 (documenting model training and selection); para 3.13, p. 29; p. 37 (data provenance record); p. 48 (traceability)
items.quote: Documenting how the model training and selection processes are conducted, the reasons for which decisions are made, and measures taken to address identified risks
items.why: International comparator. Singapore's voluntary framework treats records as the means of answering to regulators and individuals: document training and selection decisions with reasons, keep a data provenance record, and make decisions traceable. It is written for private companies and covers the whole system, not only personal data. Limits: voluntary, not UK law, and published in January 2020 before generative AI. Release date as given in its summary of updates (p. 4).

items.title: Reviewable Automated Decision-Making: A Framework for Accountable Algorithmic Systems
items.publisher: arXiv (J. Cobbe, M. S. A. Lee and J. Singh; ACM FAccT 2021)
items.quote: determining the contextually appropriate record-keeping mechanisms to facilitate meaningful review
items.why: Peer-reviewed research that gives the criterion its theory. Explanations of a model are not enough for a regulator or court; what is needed is a record of the whole decision process, human and technical, from commissioning to consequences, designed so that an outsider can review individual decisions and the process. Draws on how administrative law reviews human decisions. Limits: abstract only read in this pass; a framework, not an empirical test; the authors' copy, conference as stated on the arXiv page.

items.title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
items.publisher: arXiv (I. D. Raji and others; ACM FAT* 2020)
items.quote: Each stage of the audit yields a set of documents that together form an overall audit report
items.why: Peer-reviewed research on building the file as the work is done. Proposes an internal audit running through the whole development cycle, each stage leaving documents that together form the audit report, because once a system is live problems can be 'difficult or impossible to trace back to their source'. Supports the brief's point that records must be made at the time and not assembled on request. Limits: abstract only read in this pass; a proposed method, not evidence that it works.
